title: THE MOST DANGEROUS ADVICE YOU MAY HAVE EVER BELIEVED: “JUST FOLLOW YOUR HEART”
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS ADVICE YOU MAY HAVE EVER BELIEVED: “JUST FOLLOW YOUR HEART”

What if the voice you’ve trusted most is the very voice leading you away from God? The Bible reveals a truth that could break your heart, save your soul, and completely change the direction of your life.
There is a sentence that has destroyed marriages without ever sounding cruel.

It has led people into relationships they knew were wrong, convinced believers to abandon convictions they once held sacred, and persuaded wounded souls to mistake temporary happiness for lasting peace.
And the frightening part?
It sounds beautiful.
It sounds empowering.
Sometimes, it even sounds spiritual.
“Just follow your heart.”
You have heard it in movies. You have seen it written beneath beautiful photographs. You have probably heard it from someone who genuinely loved you and wanted you to be happy.
Perhaps you have even said it to yourself.
“I deserve to be happy.”
“God knows my heart.”
“It feels so right. How could it possibly be wrong?”
But what happens when the thing your heart desperately wants is the very thing God is asking you to surrender?
What happens when your emotions are screaming yes, but Scripture is quietly saying no?
What happens when following your heart means walking away from the One who gave you life?
There is a reason Jesus never made personal feelings the final authority for His disciples.
And there is a reason the Bible speaks about the human heart with both extraordinary tenderness and terrifying honesty.
Because the heart can love deeply.
The heart can grieve sincerely.
The heart can desire beautiful things.
But the heart can also deceive the very person carrying it.

And somewhere between the wounds you never healed, the desires you never questioned, and the decisions you justified because they felt right, you may have begun trusting your heart more than the voice of God.
Please stay with me.
Because this is not an article about learning to hate your emotions.
It is about discovering why Jesus came to give you something far greater than permission to follow them.
He came to give you a new heart.
And understanding that difference could change everything.
Imagine a woman sitting alone in her car outside her home.
The engine is off.
Her phone is glowing in her hand.
A message has just arrived from someone who makes her feel noticed, valued, and understood in ways she has not felt for years.
She is married.
She knows the conversation has crossed boundaries.
She knows the secrecy is growing.
She knows there are things she would never want her husband to discover.
But she is lonely.
And loneliness has a way of making dangerous attention feel like answered prayer.
She stares at the message.
Her heart races.
Then comes the thought.
“Maybe God just wants me to be happy.”
And suddenly, what began as temptation starts looking like destiny.
Now imagine a young man exhausted from trying to do the right thing.
He has watched dishonest people prosper while his integrity seems to cost him opportunities.
One day, someone offers him a shortcut.
Just one compromise.
Just one lie.
Just one decision nobody needs to know about.
His conscience hesitates.
But his heart whispers, “You have suffered enough. You deserve this.”
And he begins negotiating with something God has already made clear.
Different stories.
Different wounds.
Different temptations.
The same dangerous possibility.
A sincere feeling can become a convincing excuse.
Not because every feeling is sinful.
Not because every desire is corrupt.
But because sincerity is not the same as truth.
And the fact that something feels deeply personal does not make it divinely approved.
Thousands of years before motivational speakers began telling the world to trust every inward impulse, the prophet Jeremiah recorded a warning that still confronts the human soul.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9, KJV
That verse is uncomfortable.
Especially in a generation that often treats personal authenticity as the highest form of morality.
But let us look more closely at what Scripture actually says.
In the Hebrew text, the verse begins:
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿĀqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl wəʾānuš hûʾ mî yēḏāʿennû
A careful rendering is:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?”
The Hebrew word ʿāqōḇ carries the sense of something deceptive, crooked, or treacherous.
The word lēḇ, translated “heart,” refers to more than emotion. In biblical Hebrew, the heart is the inner center of human thought, desire, intention, and decision-making.
And ʾānuš can describe something desperately sick or incurable.

The King James Version uses “desperately wicked,” while several modern translations use “desperately sick.” The latter reflects the sickness imagery in the Hebrew more directly, without denying the moral seriousness of the passage.
But notice something essential.
Jeremiah was not writing a random insult against human emotions.
The surrounding chapter contrasts those who trust in human strength with those whose confidence rests in the Lord.
Jeremiah 17:5 warns against making flesh one's strength while turning the heart away from God.
Jeremiah 17:7 declares:
“Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.”
Then comes the warning about the deceitful heart.
The issue is not whether human beings are capable of genuine love, compassion, or joy.
The issue is whether the fallen human heart can safely become its own ultimate authority.
Scripture's answer is no.
And Jeremiah does not leave us guessing about who truly understands the heart.
The very next verse says:
“I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.” — Jeremiah 17:10, KJV
The God who knows the heart better than we know ourselves is also the God before whom our motives and actions are exposed.
That should humble us.
Because sometimes we do not merely hide the truth from other people.
Sometimes we become extraordinarily skilled at hiding it from ourselves.
We call pride self-respect.
We call bitterness having boundaries.
We call lust chemistry.
We call revenge justice.
We call disobedience finding ourselves.
And sometimes we call our unwillingness to surrender following our hearts.
Of course, boundaries can be necessary. Justice matters. Love and attraction are not inherently sinful. And protecting yourself from abuse is not rebellion against God.
The danger begins when we use otherwise meaningful words to disguise what Scripture calls sin.
That is how self-deception works.
It rarely announces itself.
It usually offers an explanation that makes us feel innocent.
And before long, we can become more committed to defending our desires than examining them.
Have you ever prayed for God to guide you while secretly hoping He would approve the decision you had already made?
Have you ever asked Him for a sign while avoiding the Scripture that already addressed your situation?
Have you ever called something peace simply because you felt relieved after choosing what you wanted?
I have a question worth sitting with.
What if the reason you cannot hear God's answer is that you have already decided which answer you are willing to accept?
That question is not meant to crush you.
It is meant to invite honesty.
Because Jesus does not heal the person we pretend to be.
He meets us in the truth about who we actually are.
And this is where the story becomes even more personal.
The problem is not simply that we sometimes make poor decisions.
According to Jesus, sin reaches deeper than behavior.
It touches the inner life from which behavior grows.
In Mark 7:20–23, Jesus explains that evil thoughts and sinful actions come from within the human person.
He names things we would rather keep hidden: sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, covetousness, deceit, pride, and foolishness.
Jesus was confronting the mistaken belief that outward religious cleanliness could substitute for inward holiness.
And in doing so, He exposed something that religious people and irreligious people alike need to understand.
You can look respectable while your heart is drifting.
You can know worship songs while secretly nurturing resentment.
You can post Bible verses while entertaining desires you refuse to bring before God.
You can serve in church and still be controlled by pride.
You can speak about grace while resisting repentance.
You can even become so accustomed to appearing spiritually healthy that you forget how desperately you need the Great Physician.
But here is where many people misunderstand the Gospel.
Jesus did not expose the human heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposed the human heart because He came to save sinners.
The diagnosis was never the end of the story.
And if you have already begun thinking about the compromises you regret, the people you hurt, the relationships you damaged, or the years you spent running from God, please do not stop reading here.
Because the most beautiful part of this truth is still ahead.
The Bible does not merely tell us that our hearts can deceive us.
It tells us that God can transform them.
Centuries before the birth of Jesus, the Lord spoke through Ezekiel to a people marked by rebellion, idolatry, exile, and spiritual failure.
They had broken covenant.
They had dishonored His name.
They had experienced the devastating consequences of their sin.
Yet God announced a promise that would reach beyond outward religious reform.
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” — Ezekiel 36:26, KJV
In Hebrew, the promise begins:
וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ
Wənāṯattî lāḵem lēḇ ḥāḏāš
“And I will give you a new heart.”
Notice the direction of the promise.
God does not say, “Find your true heart and obey whatever it tells you.”
He says, “I will give you a new heart.”
The Hebrew ḥāḏāš means “new.”
And the image of a heart of flesh replacing a heart of stone speaks of a heart made responsive rather than hardened toward God.
This promise was first spoken in the context of God's restoration of Israel, and it belongs to Ezekiel's larger vision of covenant renewal, cleansing, and the work of God's Spirit.
Christians understand this promised renewal in light of the new covenant accomplished through Jesus Christ and the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
The next verse makes the connection to obedience unmistakable.
“And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.” — Ezekiel 36:27, KJV
Do you see the beauty?
God does not merely command His people to become different.
He promises to work within them.
This is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
This is divine transformation.
This is the difference between trying to make an unrenewed heart your compass and receiving a new life directed by the Spirit of God.
And this is why the message of Jesus is so much greater than the popular advice to follow your heart.
Jesus does not simply affirm every desire you bring to Him.
Sometimes He confronts it.
Sometimes He calls you to surrender it.
Sometimes He exposes the false promise hiding beneath it.
But He does so as the Savior who gave Himself to redeem you.
There is a difference between a God who wants to control your life for His amusement and a Savior who loves you enough to rescue you from what is destroying you.
The Gospel reveals the latter.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was publicly accused of adultery.
Her shame was exposed before a crowd.
The religious leaders wanted to use her case to trap Jesus.
And there she stood, a human being reduced to the worst thing she had done.
Perhaps you know something about that feeling.
Not the exact circumstances.
But the shame.
The memory.
The fear that if people knew the whole story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Maybe you have made decisions you cannot undo.
Maybe you trusted someone you should not have trusted.
Maybe you betrayed someone who loved you.
Maybe you have spent years carrying a secret that still makes your stomach tighten whenever the past comes to mind.
And perhaps you have wondered whether God looks at you with the same disgust you imagine in everyone else's eyes.
Listen carefully to what happens in the biblical account.
Jesus confronts the accusers' hypocrisy.
One by one, they leave.
Then Jesus speaks to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV

A textual note matters here: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, and modern Bibles commonly identify this passage as a later textual addition. It should therefore not be treated as the sole foundation for a doctrine. Its portrayal of mercy joined with a call away from sin, however, agrees with teaching clearly found elsewhere in the New Testament, including Romans 8:1 and Titus 2:11–12.
And the message is unmistakable when we consider the whole witness of Scripture.
Grace does not mean sin is harmless.
Repentance does not mean forgiveness must be earned.
Jesus does not offer condemnation as the final word to those who belong to Him.
And He does not offer permission to remain enslaved to the very things He came to redeem us from.
He offers mercy that calls us into a changed life.
That is the Gospel.
Not “Follow your heart wherever it leads.”
Not “Pretend your heart has never wanted anything wrong.”
But come to Christ with your sin, your shame, your confusion, your desires, your wounds, and your need for mercy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting the Savior who died and rose again.
And let His grace begin changing what you love.
Because the deepest Christian transformation is not merely doing the right thing while secretly wishing you could keep doing wrong.
It is the Spirit of God renewing your desires so that obedience becomes an expression of love for Christ.
This does not happen perfectly or instantly.
Believers still struggle.
Temptation still exists.
Old habits can return.
Some wounds require patient care, wise counsel, accountability, and time.
But the presence of a struggle does not mean God's transforming work is imaginary.
And the fact that you still need grace does not mean grace has failed.
The apostle Paul describes the conflict of the Christian life in Galatians 5:16–17.
He calls believers to walk by the Spirit rather than gratify the desires of the flesh.

Here the Greek word sarx, commonly translated “flesh,” does not simply mean the physical body or ordinary human emotion. In this context, it refers to human nature in its opposition to the Spirit's work.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not a command to become emotionless.
Jesus Himself experienced deep sorrow.
He wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
He felt compassion for suffering people.
In Gethsemane, He spoke openly of His overwhelming anguish.
Emotions are not the enemy.
They are part of our created humanity.
But emotions are not infallible guides.
You can feel afraid and still obey God.
You can feel lonely and still remain faithful.
You can feel angry and refuse to sin.
You can feel attracted to someone and choose purity.
You can feel exhausted and ask for help without abandoning your convictions.
You can grieve deeply and still trust the Lord.
And sometimes, the most courageous act of faith is to tell God:
“Lord, this is what I feel. This is what I want. But more than anything, I want Your will.”
That is not dishonesty.
That is surrender.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
Jesus was without sin, so His prayer was not a confession of sinful desire. It was the sinless Son's willing submission to the Father's will in the face of real suffering.
And in that perfect obedience, we see what surrendered trust looks like.
Not the absence of pain.
Not the denial of feeling.
But faithfulness when obedience is costly.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
You know what Scripture teaches.
You know what obedience would require.
But your heart is attached to something you are afraid to lose.
A relationship.
A habit.
A hidden conversation.
A source of validation.
A dream that has become more important than the God who gave you life.
Or perhaps your struggle looks nothing like those things.
Perhaps your heart is telling you that you are worthless.
That you will never recover.
That your mistakes have permanently disqualified you from being loved.
That because someone abandoned you, you must be unlovable.
That because you failed yesterday, tomorrow cannot be different.
Those feelings can be overwhelming.
But they are not the final authority over your identity either.
The same Bible that warns us about self-deception also tells believers that they are loved in Christ, forgiven through His blood, and welcomed into the family of God by grace.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
Do not allow your heart to overrule God's warnings.
But do not allow your heart to overrule His promises either.
That is an important part of spiritual maturity.
Sometimes your heart tells you that sin is safe when God says it destroys.
Sometimes your heart tells you that you are beyond mercy when God calls sinners to repent and believe.
In both cases, the answer is the same.
Trust what God has revealed above what your feelings insist.
And perhaps this is why Proverbs 3:5 speaks so directly to us.
“Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.”
Notice that Scripture does not command us to abandon the heart altogether.
It commands us to direct our trust toward the Lord with the whole heart.
The issue is not whether you should have desires.
The issue is whom your desires should serve.
The issue is not whether you should think or feel.
The issue is whether your thinking and feeling will be brought under the authority of God's truth.
Psalm 37:4 says:
“Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.”
Some people read that as a promise that God will give them whatever they happen to want.
But the verse begins with delighting in the Lord.
It is not a blank check for every ambition, romance, purchase, or personal preference.
It describes a life oriented toward God, trusting His goodness and finding joy in Him.
As we delight in the Lord, our desires are increasingly shaped by what honors Him.
That is far more beautiful than a God who merely rubber-stamps our wishes.
It is a God who teaches us to love what is truly good.
And there is another verse that belongs in this conversation.
“Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.” — Proverbs 4:23, KJV
The Hebrew instruction is:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
Mikkol-mišmār nəṣōr libbeḵā
A close sense is, “Above all guarding, guard your heart.”
The verb nāṣar, here appearing in the imperative form nəṣōr, conveys the idea of guarding, watching over, or preserving.
This is not permission to obey every impulse.
It is a call to exercise careful stewardship over the inner life.
Guard what you allow to shape your affections.
Guard the stories you repeatedly tell yourself.
Guard against resentment that begins to feel justified.
Guard against the temptation to confuse attention with love.
Guard against teaching that flatters your desires while avoiding the truth of Scripture.
Guard your heart, not because it is worthless, but because what happens within it profoundly affects how you live.
And guarding it does not mean building walls so high that nobody can love you.
It means allowing God's wisdom to shape what you welcome, what you resist, what you believe, and what you pursue.
But let me speak to the person who has already followed their heart into a place they never intended to go.
The one who wishes they could rewind time.
The one who has said, “If only I had listened.”
The one who knows exactly what it feels like to mistake excitement for love, stubbornness for courage, or self-indulgence for freedom.
You cannot change yesterday.
You cannot erase every consequence.
You may need to confess, apologize, make restitution, seek accountability, or rebuild trust over time.
Some relationships may not be restored in the way you hope.
Some consequences may remain even after forgiveness.
And no honest presentation of the Gospel should promise that repentance will instantly repair every earthly loss.
But your past does not have to become your master.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is reconciliation with God through His Son.
There is the possibility of a new direction, even when the road ahead requires humility, patience, and difficult obedience.
Listen to the apostle Paul's words.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
The Greek phrase is:
καινὴ κτίσις
Kainē ktisis
“New creation.”
The word kainos emphasizes newness in quality or character, and ktisis means creation.
Paul is not promising that every painful memory will disappear or that every consequence of sin will vanish overnight.
He is describing the profound new reality of belonging to Christ.
In the surrounding passage, Paul explains that this new life comes through God's reconciling work in Jesus.
And in verse 21, he declares that God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Here is the center of everything.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make you feel better about yourself.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He lived in perfect obedience where we have failed.
He died for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and new life are proclaimed to all who repent and believe.
Your heart cannot save you.
Your sincerity cannot save you.
Your religious performance cannot save you.
Your emotional intensity cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
That is why the answer to a deceitful heart is not despair.
It is the Savior.
The answer to shame is not pretending sin never mattered.
It is the cross where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's mercy meet.
The answer to spiritual emptiness is not another inspirational slogan.
It is reconciliation with the living God.
And the answer to the question, “Should I follow my heart?” is not a simplistic rejection of every human desire.
It is something much deeper.
Follow Jesus, and let Him teach your heart where to go.
When your heart agrees with His truth, walk in gratitude.
When your heart resists His truth, surrender in faith.
When your heart is wounded, bring it to Him for healing.
When your heart is proud, ask Him for humility.
When your heart is confused, seek wisdom through Scripture, prayer, and mature Christian counsel.
When your heart is tempted, do not pretend the temptation is harmless.
And when your heart condemns you despite genuine repentance and faith in Christ, remember that His promises are more reliable than your changing emotions.
You do not need to manufacture perfect feelings before you obey.
You need the grace of God to take the next faithful step.
Sometimes that step is ending a secret relationship.
Sometimes it is telling the truth.
Sometimes it is asking someone to forgive you.
Sometimes it is seeking help for a destructive pattern.
Sometimes it is refusing to return to a situation that is abusive or dangerous.
Sometimes it is opening your Bible again after months of avoiding it.
Sometimes it is praying through tears because you have no idea how to begin.
And sometimes it is simply whispering:
“Jesus, I have trusted my own heart more than I have trusted You. Please forgive me. Teach me to follow You.”
That prayer does not earn salvation.
But it can express the humility of a heart turning toward the Savior.
And perhaps someone reading this has never truly entrusted their life to Christ.
You have known about Jesus.
You have admired His teachings.
You may even have grown up in church.
But deep inside, you have been living as though the final authority belongs to you.
Today, hear His invitation.
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
The Greek word translated “repent” is metanoeite, from metanoeō, referring to a change of mind and direction, a turning that involves the whole person.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling guilty.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And saving faith is more than agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting Him as Savior and Lord.
You cannot purchase that grace.
You cannot earn it through donations, church attendance, or religious activity.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Never forget that.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's forgiveness is not a reward for financial support.
And the love of Christ cannot be measured by the size of an offering.
Everything begins with grace.
And genuine grace changes how we live, love, give, serve, and care for others.
That is also why sharing biblical truth matters.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be living through the very struggle described here.
Someone may be preparing to make a decision that could wound their family.
Someone may be mistaking an unhealthy attachment for love.
Someone may be carrying unbearable shame and believing there is no way back to God.
You may never know what a single article, shared at the right moment, could mean to someone who is quietly searching for hope.
Not to prove you are more spiritual than anyone else.
Not to publicly shame someone whose choices concern you.
But because truth offered with compassion can reach people who might never walk through the doors of a church.

And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with kindness, provided doing so would not expose a private struggle or embarrass them. Sometimes a private message is the more loving choice.
You do not have to write a sermon.
You can simply say, “I thought this was worth reading.”
And perhaps you have your own story.
Maybe you followed your heart and discovered that what you wanted was not what you needed.
Maybe you resisted temptation and learned that obedience, though painful at first, protected you from greater sorrow.
Maybe you are still struggling to surrender something.
Maybe you have experienced God's mercy after a season of rebellion.
You can simply write:
Or, if you are in a difficult season:
“Pray for me. I'm learning to surrender.”
You do not need to reveal anything private or unsafe. You do not need to perform vulnerability for strangers.
But sometimes a few sincere words remind another believer that they are not the only one fighting to remain faithful.
Your testimony may encourage someone.
Your request for prayer may give others an opportunity to care.
And your willingness to be honest may remind a struggling Christian that growth in Christ is not always a straight line.
Because there may come another day when your feelings are loud, your judgment is clouded, and the easiest path seems more attractive than the faithful one.
On that day, remember:
A strong feeling is not necessarily God's leading.
An open door is not automatically God's approval.
A difficult command is not evidence that God has stopped loving you.
And surrendering something you want is not always losing something good.
Sometimes it is the beginning of freedom.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not religious entertainment.
Not spiritual slogans designed to flatter us.
But biblical truth that points people back to Jesus Christ, calls us to repentance, reminds us of grace, and encourages us to grow in faithful discipleship.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still exploring the Christian faith.
Let them encounter the Scriptures.
Let them ask questions.
Let them discover that Christianity is not ultimately about pretending to be perfect, but about knowing the perfect Savior who redeems sinners and transforms lives.
And if these articles have strengthened your faith, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is continuing the work of producing Christ-centered articles, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources that help people engage more seriously with God's Word.
These resources are part of a mission to make biblical nourishment and discipleship more accessible.
And maintaining, developing, and expanding that work requires time, effort, and practical support.
Think of it as a voluntary act of generosity toward a ministry whose work you believe is worth sustaining.
Scripture teaches that those who receive spiritual instruction may share good things with those who teach (Galatians 6:6), and that Christian giving should be willing rather than pressured.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
It should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe or presented as a replacement for your responsibilities to your local church, family, or others in need.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience, love, service, generosity, and a life increasingly shaped by His Word.
These items are not the Gospel itself.
They are simply practical resources and expressions of encouragement that can accompany a life of discipleship.
There is no pressure to give beyond your means.
Sometimes the person who shares a message reaches someone the writer could never reach.
Sometimes a quiet act of encouragement becomes part of another person's journey back to Scripture.
And sometimes faithful ministry support helps ensure that biblical teaching remains available to people who cannot afford to pay for it.
That is a beautiful reason to give freely, when you are able.
Not about money.
Not about engagement.
Not about what anyone else will think.
Just you and God.
Who has been leading your life?
Your fears?
Your wounds?
Your cravings?
Your need for approval?
Your longing to be loved?
Your determination never to be hurt again?
Or Jesus Christ?
Because at the end of the day, the greatest danger of “follow your heart” is not that you might make an embarrassing decision.
It is that you might spend your life treating your own desires as lord while leaving the true Lord standing outside the decisions that matter most.
And the greatest beauty of the Gospel is that Jesus came to rescue people who have done exactly that.
People like Peter, who denied Him.
People like Paul, who once persecuted His church.
People like the tax collectors and sinners who discovered that the Messiah had come to call them to repentance.
People like us.
People whose hearts have wandered.
People whose motives have been mixed.
People who have loved the wrong things too much and loved God too little.
Yet the invitation remains.
Turn to Christ.
Trust His Word.
Receive His mercy.
Walk by His Spirit.
Let Him renew what sin has distorted.
Let Him teach you that true freedom is not being ruled by every desire that rises within you.
True freedom is belonging to the One who created you, knows you, loves you, and gave Himself to redeem you.
So the next time someone tells you, “Just follow your heart,” remember that Scripture gives you a better invitation.
Do not make your heart your god.
Bring your heart to God.
And follow Jesus.
Because the heart that once led you into darkness can, by God's renewing grace, learn to love the Light.
If this truth reached a place in you that you have kept hidden, do not ignore it.
Talk to the Lord about it today.
May that be more than a sentence beneath an article.
May it become the direction of your life.
The heart that once helped write your greatest regret does not have to write the ending of your story—because Jesus Christ is still making broken lives new.
